claim: Bacteriophage λ uses E. coli's outer-membrane protein LamB as its native receptor.
source: λ's native receptor is E. coli's outer-membrane protein LamB, but through mutations in its host-recognition gene J, λ evolves to use a second receptor protein, OmpF.
evidence: This is stated directly in the manuscript as established background information about the λ-E. coli system.

claim: Through mutations in gene J, bacteriophage λ can evolve to use OmpF as a second receptor protein.
source: λ's native receptor is E. coli's outer-membrane protein LamB, but through mutations in its host-recognition gene J, λ evolves to use a second receptor protein, OmpF.
evidence: This is stated directly and is supported by previous research cited in the manuscript (Meyer et al., 2012).

claim: Only four mutations are necessary for λ to gain OmpF+ function.
source: While only four mutations are necessary for OmpF+ function (Maddamsetti et al., 2018), more J mutations typically evolve along the way (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Maddamsetti et al., 2018.

claim: E. coli evolves resistance to λ through malT mutations that cause reduced LamB expression.
source: λ gains this new function after E. coli evolves resistance through malT mutations (Meyer et al., 2012) that cause reduced LamB expression (Boos and Böhm, 2000).
evidence: This is supported by citations to Meyer et al., 2012 and Boos and Böhm, 2000.

claim: The fitness landscape of λ with the ancestral host has a diminishing-returns pattern.
source: Visual inspection of the two fitness landscapes reveals host-dependent structures; the landscape with the ancestral host has a standard diminishing-returns pattern (Khan et al., 2011; Chou et al., 2011; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014; MacLean et al., 2010; Guerrero et al., 2019), while the landscape with the malT— host has an atypical sigmoidal shape that plateaus at a higher fitness than the first (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of Figure 1a and comparison to patterns described in cited literature.

claim: The fitness landscape of λ with the malT− host has an atypical sigmoidal shape that plateaus at a higher fitness than the ancestral host landscape.
source: Visual inspection of the two fitness landscapes reveals host-dependent structures; the landscape with the ancestral host has a standard diminishing-returns pattern (Khan et al., 2011; Chou et al., 2011; Kryazhimskiy et al., 2014; MacLean et al., 2010; Guerrero et al., 2019), while the landscape with the malT— host has an atypical sigmoidal shape that plateaus at a higher fitness than the first (Figure 1a and b).
evidence: This is based on visual inspection of Figure 1b and comparison to the ancestral landscape.

claim: There are significant mutation-by-host interactions in λ's fitness landscape.
source: In this model, we found significant mutation-by-host interactions (Figure 1d), and sizeable effects of the host-dependent epistasis (21 mutation-by-mutation-by-host interaction terms were significant out of 45 and 12.62% of the total variance in the data were attributable to these terms, Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on regression analysis that included host as a predictor variable, with results shown in Figure 1d.

claim: 21 out of 45 mutation-by-mutation-by-host interaction terms were significant, accounting for 12.62% of total variance.
source: In this model, we found significant mutation-by-host interactions (Figure 1d), and sizeable effects of the host-dependent epistasis (21 mutation-by-mutation-by-host interaction terms were significant out of 45 and 12.62% of the total variance in the data were attributable to these terms, Figure 1d).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of the combined fitness landscape model.

claim: A combinatorial library of 671 λ genotypes out of a possible 1024 was successfully engineered using MAGE.
source: Using Multiplexed Automated Genome Engineering (MAGE) (Wang et al., 2009), a technique that uses repeated cycles of homologous recombination in the λ-red system to produce combinatorial genomic diversity, we were successful at engineering a library of 671 genotypes out of the possible 1024 (see Materials and methods).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental outcome of the MAGE procedure.

claim: Fitness was measured for 580 λ genotypes cocultured with ancestral E. coli and 131 genotypes with malT−.
source: Overall, we were able to measure the fitness of 580 λ genotypes cocultured with ancestral E. coli and 131 genotypes with malT– (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement of the number of genotypes successfully measured in each condition.

claim: Shifting landscape protocols increased the frequency of OmpF+ evolution above single host simulations in all nine treatments.
source: As anticipated, the switching protocol increased the frequency of OmpF+ evolution in all nine treatments above the single host simulations, but only seven out of nine treatments were found to be significantly higher (Figure 2; ANOVA: F-ratio=6.14, d.f.=99, p<0.0001, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is based on simulation results shown in Figure 2 and statistical analysis.

claim: Seven out of nine shifting landscape treatments showed significantly higher OmpF+ evolution compared to single host simulations.
source: As anticipated, the switching protocol increased the frequency of OmpF+ evolution in all nine treatments above the single host simulations, but only seven out of nine treatments were found to be significantly higher (Figure 2; ANOVA: F-ratio=6.14, d.f.=99, p<0.0001, Supplementary file 1b).
evidence: This is based on statistical analysis of simulation results with ANOVA and post-hoc testing.

claim: The first mutation on the line of descent to OmpF+ (mutation A) required ancestral E. coli to evolve.
source: We found that the first mutation on the line of descent to OmpF+ required ancestral E. coli to evolve, while the second mutation required malT– E. coli (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is based on pairwise competition experiments shown in Figure 3b and c.

claim: The second mutation on the line of descent to OmpF+ (mutation B) required malT− E. coli to evolve.
source: We found that the first mutation on the line of descent to OmpF+ required ancestral E. coli to evolve, while the second mutation required malT– E. coli (Figure 3b and c).
evidence: This is based on pairwise competition experiments shown in Figure 3b and c.

claim: malT− E. coli was not significantly more fit than ancestral E. coli in the presence of ancestral λ.
source: We found that malT– was not significantly more fit than the ancestral E. coli in the presence of the ancestral λ, but it was more fit in the presence of the evolved λs (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is based on competition experiments between host genotypes in the presence of different λ genotypes, shown in Figure 3d.

claim: malT− E. coli was more fit than ancestral E. coli in the presence of evolved λ genotypes.
source: We found that malT– was not significantly more fit than the ancestral E. coli in the presence of the ancestral λ, but it was more fit in the presence of the evolved λs (Figure 3d).
evidence: This is based on competition experiments shown in Figure 3d.

claim: Zero out of 12 replicate populations evolved OmpF use when coevolution was initiated with malT− host.
source: In line with our expectations, 0 of 12 replicates evolved OmpF use in the malT– treatment, meanwhile 3 out of 12 evolved the innovation in the ancestral treatment (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental outcomes from the replay experiments.

claim: Three out of 12 replicate populations evolved OmpF use when coevolution was initiated with ancestral host.
source: In line with our expectations, 0 of 12 replicates evolved OmpF use in the malT– treatment, meanwhile 3 out of 12 evolved the innovation in the ancestral treatment (Figure 4a and b).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental outcomes from the replay experiments.

claim: Fewer J mutations evolved in λ when coevolution was initiated with malT− host compared to ancestral host.
source: By sequencing J alleles of the resulting λ genotypes, we found that fewer mutations evolved with malT– despite evolving for the same length of time.
evidence: This is based on sequencing analysis of evolved λ genotypes from the replay experiments.

claim: 16 of 24 λ populations evolved OmpF+ when initiated with λ strains positioned one or two mutations away from OmpF+ function.
source: We initiated two more replays: one with a λ strain that was just a single mutation away from becoming OmpF+, and another that was two mutations away (see Supplementary file 1f for J alleles). 16 of 24 λ populations evolved OmpF+ showing that whether malT– promotes OmpF+ evolution depends on where the λ genotypes are located in the fitness landscape (Figure 4c and d).
evidence: This is a direct report of experimental outcomes from replay experiments with partially evolved λ strains.

claim: λ initially evolves mutations in J that enhance its infectivity before E. coli evolves resistance.
source: λ is initially poor at infecting its host, so it evolves mutations in J that enhance its infectivity. The new λ genotypes apply pressure on E. coli to evolve resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the phylogenetic reconstruction and competition experiments showing the temporal sequence of mutations.

claim: The new λ genotypes with enhanced infectivity apply pressure on E. coli to evolve resistance.
source: The new λ genotypes apply pressure on E. coli to evolve resistance.
evidence: This is inferred from the competition experiments showing that malT− becomes more fit in the presence of evolved λ genotypes.

claim: When host-resistance increases in the community, λ's fitness landscape is deformed in a way that promotes J evolution toward OmpF use, but only if λ had already acquired some J mutations.
source: When host-resistance increases in the community, λ's fitness landscape is deformed in a way that promotes J evolution toward OmpF use, but only if it had already acquired some J mutations.
evidence: This is inferred from the combination of simulation results, competition experiments, and replay experiments showing contingency on prior mutations.

claim: The timing and coordination of coevolutionary steps is facilitated by the reciprocity ingrained in host-parasite coevolution.
source: Remarkably, the timing and coordination of each of these interdependent steps is facilitated by the reciprocity ingrained in host-parasite coevolution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing the interdependence of host and parasite evolution.

claim: Coevolution can promote evolutionary innovations by deforming fitness landscapes in ways that open new adaptive pathways.
source: Theory suggests that coevolution between species can promote the evolution of such innovations by deforming fitness landscapes in ways that open new adaptive pathways.
evidence: This is stated as theoretical background and is tested by the experiments in the manuscript.

claim: The probability of observing no OmpF+ evolution in 12 replicate populations with ancestral host is approximately 0.03, given λ's established one in four rate of OmpF+ evolution.
source: Given λ's established one in four rates of OmpF+ with ancestral host, the probability of observing no OmpF+ evolution in 12 replicate populations is ~0.03.
evidence: This is a statistical calculation based on a binomial distribution and previously established rates.

claim: λ's mutation rate is 7.7×10−8 per base per replication.
source: The simulations were run based on conservative estimates of the number of generations and population sizes from previously published (Meyer et al., 2012) and this study's coevolution experiments (960 generations; ~6.3×109 λ particles, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Meyer et al., 2012) and λ's intrinsic mutation rate (7.7×10–8 base–1 replication–1) (Drake, 1991).
evidence: This is cited from Drake, 1991.

claim: OmpF+ genotypes must have three specific mutations: A3034G, G3319A, and T3321A, plus one additional mutation.
source: They all possess two specific changes (A3034G) and (G3319A) and a third change that can occur at positions 3320 or 3321. For the 10 mutations we studied, T3321A is the only third mutation that satisfies this requirement, meaning all OmpF genotypes must have three specific changes (A3034G, G3319A, and T3321A). Many J mutations satisfy the last requirement (Maddamsetti et al., 2018), so we implemented what we call the '3+1' rule where genotypes are designated as OmpF+ if they have the three necessary J mutations plus any additional mutation (see Supplementary file 1i).
evidence: This is based on previous research (Maddamsetti et al., 2018) and defines the criteria used in the simulations.

claim: The ancestral phage λ strain used in the study is cI26, a strictly lytic strain.
source: The ancestral phage λ strain in our study is cI26; it is a strictly lytic strain that was used in the previous coevolution study on which this paper builds (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental materials used.

claim: The cI26 strain has a frameshift mutation in the cI gene that disrupts the regulatory protein cI required for lysogenic life cycle.
source: The λ strain cI26 has a frameshift mutation in the cI gene that disrupts the regulatory protein cI required by λ to switch to a lysogenic life cycle (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the strain used, with citation to Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: E. coli B strain REL606 was used as the ancestral-sensitive host.
source: We used E. coli B strain REL606 for the ancestral-sensitive host and its derivative EcC4 for the evolved-resistant (malT–) host to construct fitness landscapes (in Figure 1) and run competition assays (in Figure 3).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental materials used.

claim: EcC4 has a single nonsense mutation (C→T) at genome location 3,482,567 in the malT gene.
source: REL606 was the ancestral host in the coevolution experiments performed by Meyer et al., 2012, and EcC4 was isolated from one of the coevolving populations that has a single mutation, a nonsense mutation (C→T) at genome location 3,482,567 in malT gene (Table S5 in Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is stated as a characteristic of the strain, with citation to Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: A disruption in transcription of malT inhibits LamB expression.
source: MalT is a positive regulator of lamB, so a disruption in transcription of malT inhibits LamB expression (Boos and Böhm, 2000).
evidence: This is stated with citation to Boos and Böhm, 2000.

claim: Watermark mutations were used to distinguish between true genome edits and sequencing errors.
source: To improve our resolution, we edited a synonymous mutation adjacent to each focal mutation. We called this a watermark mutation because it helped us distinguish between a true genome edit and an error in sequencing. By only recording the presence of a focal mutation if it occurred alongside the watermark, we decreased our detection limit from ~10–3 to ~10–6.
evidence: This is a direct description of the methodological approach used.

claim: The watermark strategy decreased the detection limit from approximately 10−3 to 10−6.
source: By only recording the presence of a focal mutation if it occurred alongside the watermark, we decreased our detection limit from ~10–3 to ~10–6.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the improvement in detection sensitivity.

claim: The λ genomic library and ancestral λ were cocultured in a 1:9 ratio for fitness measurements.
source: To do this, we cocultured the λ genomic library and ancestral λ in a 1:9 ratio.
evidence: This is a direct description of the experimental protocol.

claim: Competitions were run for 4 hours to measure λ fitness.
source: Flasks were cultured for 4 hr at 37°C and shaking at 120 rpm.
evidence: This is a direct statement of the experimental protocol.

claim: An average of 107,839 high quality reads per sample were obtained from Illumina sequencing, with a standard deviation of 26,889.
source: We were able to extract on average 107,839 high quality reads per sample with standard deviation of 26,889.
evidence: This is a direct report of sequencing data quality.

claim: The simulations were run for 960 generations, corresponding to two doublings per hour for a 20-day experiment.
source: Given this, we decided to run the simulation for a somewhat arbitrary amount of time, 960 generations which corresponds to two doublings per hour for the 20-day experiment we are trying to replicate Meyer et al., 2012.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation parameters.

claim: The population size used in simulations was approximately 6.3×10^9 λ particles.
source: The simulations were run based on conservative estimates of the number of generations and population sizes from previously published (Meyer et al., 2012) and this study's coevolution experiments (960 generations; ~6.3×109 λ particles, Figure 4—figure supplement 1; Meyer et al., 2012) and λ's intrinsic mutation rate (7.7×10–8 base–1 replication–1) (Drake, 1991).
evidence: This is based on estimates from previous experiments and data shown in Figure 4—figure supplement 1.

claim: The threshold for detecting OmpF+ genotypes in simulations was set at 5000 λ particles.
source: If any such genotype crossed the threshold of 5000 λ particles during the course of a simulation, the λ population in that run was marked to have evolved OmpF-function. We based the threshold value on the detection limit of OmpF+ genotypes in the original laboratory coevolution experiments (~500 pfu/ml, see 'Coevolutionary Replay Experiments' section).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation criteria based on experimental detection limits.

claim: Population 'D7' from Meyer et al., 2012 was chosen for detailed analysis because λ evolved relatively few mutations in this population.
source: Population 'D7' was chosen because λ evolved relatively few mutations in this population.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the rationale for selecting this population.

claim: J evolved within a day in the coevolution experiment.
source: However, J evolved within a day, while malT— mutations were previously shown to fix between 5 and 8 days in the population (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is based on the phylogenetic reconstruction shown in Figure 3a.

claim: malT− mutations were previously shown to fix between 5 and 8 days in the population.
source: However, J evolved within a day, while malT— mutations were previously shown to fix between 5 and 8 days in the population (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is cited from Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: The lacZα marker has been shown to have a slight fitness effect.
source: The marker has been shown to have a slight fitness effect; however, this would not significantly influence our measurements of fitness since we observed such large differences between strains (Burmeister et al., 2016; Shao and Wang, 2008).
evidence: This is cited from Burmeister et al., 2016 and Shao and Wang, 2008.

claim: Coevolution's role in driving evolutionary novelty has not been directly tested before this study.
source: Although it has been shown that antagonistic coevolution can hasten molecular evolution of phages (Paterson et al., 2010) and lead them to broader host ranges (Hall et al., 2011), coevolution's role in unlocking unexplored regions of the fitness landscape has not been directly tested.
evidence: This is stated as a gap in the literature that this study addresses.

claim: The study provides direct experimental evidence that fluctuating landscapes can promote evolutionary innovations.
source: Altogether, we were able to provide direct experimental evidence that fluctuating landscapes, also known as fitness seascapes (Merrell, 1994), can promote evolutionary innovations.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the main finding of the study.

claim: λ's evolution to use a new receptor is repeatable because the sequence is coordinated by coevolutionary feedback.
source: Despite the stochasticity that is expected to arise in systems with substantial historical contingency (Gould, 1989; Blount et al., 2018), λ's evolution to use a new receptor is repeatable because the sequence is coordinated by coevolutionary feedback.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the experimental results showing repeatability despite contingency.

claim: Natural coevolutionary processes can repeatedly drive the evolution of viruses to achieve difficult adaptations that underlie host-range expansions.
source: First, natural coevolutionary processes can repeatedly drive the evolution of viruses to achieve difficult adaptations that underly host-range expansions.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the study's findings to broader implications.

claim: Shifting conditions can enhance the evolutionary potential of viruses.
source: We also learned that shifting conditions can enhance the evolutionary potential of viruses, suggesting that there could be additional unexpected consequences of human-caused environmental changes.
evidence: This is a speculative extrapolation from the study's findings.

claim: The fitness of a parasite depends on complex genetic interactions within its own genome and with the genomes of interacting hosts.
source: Our studies show that the fitness of a parasite depends on complex genetic interactions within its own genome and with the genomes of interacting hosts.
evidence: This is a summary statement of the findings regarding epistasis and interspecific interactions.

claim: λ is unlikely to evolve an innovation unless it participates in a particular sequence of coevolutionary steps with its host.
source: These interdependencies result in highly contingent evolution, where λ is unlikely to evolve an innovation unless it participates in a particular sequence of coevolutionary steps with its host.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the replay experiments and competition assays.

claim: High-throughput technologies can be used to untangle complex species interactions and predict evolution.
source: While coevolution may yield tangled banks of interactions, we demonstrate how high-throughput technologies can be used to untangle them and to predict evolution.
evidence: This is a summary statement about the methodological contribution of the study.

claim: The genotype of host and parasite that first encounter each other, as well as the timing of their coevolution, play an important role in determining the dynamics and endpoints of their evolution.
source: This suggests that the genotype of host and parasite that first encounter each other in nature, as well as the timing of their coevolution, play an important role in determining the dynamics and endpoints of their evolution.
evidence: This is an inference drawn from the replay experiments showing different outcomes depending on initial conditions.

claim: If the host outpaces the parasite in evolution, the parasite is unable to innovate.
source: We showed that if the host outpaces the parasite (Figure 4b; λWT and malT– E. coli), then the parasite is unable to innovate.
evidence: This is based on the replay experiment results shown in Figure 4b.

claim: When specific pairs of host and parasite genotypes are combined that are at complementary steps in coevolution, the innovation becomes possible and highly likely.
source: When specific pairs of host and parasite genotypes are combined that are at complementary steps in the coevolution, then the innovation becomes possible and even highly likely (Figure 4a, c and d; λWT and ancestral E. coli, λ–1 and malT– E. coli, and λ–2 and malT– E. coli).
evidence: This is based on the replay experiment results shown in Figure 4a, c, and d.

claim: The original coevolutionary model suggested E. coli evolves resistance first and then λ evolves OmpF use as a direct response.
source: λ was thought to evolve OmpF use as a direct response to malT– resistance (Meyer et al., 2012); however, here we learned that key steps were missing from that model.
evidence: This is stated as the previous understanding from Meyer et al., 2012.

claim: The updated coevolutionary model shows λ first evolves mutations that enhance infectivity, which then applies pressure on E. coli to evolve resistance, after which λ's fitness landscape is deformed to promote OmpF evolution.
source: λ is initially poor at infecting its host, so it evolves mutations in J that enhance its infectivity. The new λ genotypes apply pressure on E. coli to evolve resistance. When host-resistance increases in the community, λ's fitness landscape is deformed in a way that promotes J evolution toward OmpF use, but only if it had already acquired some J mutations.
evidence: This is the new model proposed based on the experimental findings of this study.

claim: MAGE was performed for 50 cycles to construct the combinatorial library.
source: Lastly, we ran the MAGE protocol for 50 cycles, which is the number of cycles a computer simulation of MAGE with an efficiency of 10% recombination efficiency per cycle predicted we would need to construct all variants.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: Six MAGE libraries were mixed together in equal frequencies to maximize diversity.
source: In the end, we mixed all six MAGE libraries together in equal frequencies to maximize diversity in the library.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: The ancestral λ genome was engineered with 6 synonymous mutations at wobble positions to enable selective amplification of library λs.
source: To avoid this, we engineered an ancestral genome with 6 synonymous mutations, where the reverse primer binds. These edits interfered with primer binding and caused selective amplification of the library λs. We edited 6 'wobble' positions: 3381 (g→t), 3384 (c→a), 3387 (c→a), 3390 (c→t) 3393 (g→a), and 3396 (c→a).
evidence: This is a direct description of the methodological approach.

claim: Two separate PCR reactions were run for each sample using unique barcodes to test for amplification bias.
source: As described in Kelsic et al., we ran two separate PCR reactions for each sample and used a unique barcode on each. This allowed us to test for amplification bias, which we did not detect (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental protocol and results shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: No amplification bias was detected in the PCR reactions.
source: This allowed us to test for amplification bias, which we did not detect (Figure 1—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is based on the comparison shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2.

claim: The error in fitness estimates of genotypes did not depend on the mean fitness value of the genotypes.
source: The error in fitness estimates of the genotypes did not depend on the mean fitness value of the genotypes (Figure 1—figure supplement 4).
evidence: This is based on analysis shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 4.

claim: Benjamini-Hochberg procedure was used to control for false discovery rates in identifying statistically significant terms.
source: After fitting the model, we used Benjamini-Hochberg procedure (Benjamini and Hochberg, 1995) to control for false discovery rates and identify statistically significant terms in the model (see Figure 1c).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical methods used.

claim: AIC was used to test for overfitting in the regression model.
source: Since the fit of a model generally improves as the number of predictor variables increases, we tested for overfitting using Akaike information criterion (AIC) (Akaike, 1974).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the statistical methods used.

claim: The reduced model after AIC optimization had 77 terms out of a total 111 terms.
source: We minimized AIC value using the step function in R Development Core Team, 2019 to uncover subsets of predictor variables that have high predictive power. This resulted in a more parsimonious model (77 terms out of a total 111, see Figure 1d).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the results of model selection.

claim: Missing genotype fitness values were imputed by assigning them the average fitness of their nearest neighbors.
source: A genotype with a missing fitness value was randomly chosen and assigned the mean of the fitness values of its nearest neighbors (one-mutation away genotypes) present in the landscape. This was iterated until the full genotypic space was complete.
evidence: This is a direct description of the imputation method used in simulations.

claim: 300 simulation trials were run for each treatment in the Wright-Fisher model.
source: 300 simulation trials were run for each treatment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the simulation protocol.

claim: 66 phages were isolated in total from population D7 for phylogenetic reconstruction.
source: We isolated 66 phages in total (Supplementary file 1c and d) and sequenced the full-length J gene from each in order to reconstruct the evolutionary dynamics (Figure 3a).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental procedure.

claim: Three replicate competitions were run for each treatment in the phage competition assays.
source: Three replicate competitions were run for each treatment.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: Competitions between phage genotypes were run for a single 24 hour period.
source: We competed three pairs of phages, WTlacZ vs A, A vs ABlacZ, and ABlacZ vs ABCDE, under two conditions: with ancestral E. coli or malT–. Competitions were run for a single 24 hr period under identical conditions in which the phage evolved (Meyer et al., 2012).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: Host competition assays were run for 4 hours to prevent λ from evolving during the competition.
source: The competition was performed with identical conditions as the original evolution experiment and run for 4 hr to prevent λ from evolving during the competition assay.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental protocol and its rationale.

claim: The coevolutionary replay experiments were run for 31 days.
source: The two differences were that the study was run longer (31 days) and daily estimates of λ populations were made (Figure 4—figure supplement 2).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental protocol.

claim: Twelve replicate populations were initiated for each treatment in the replay experiments.
source: We initiated 12 replicate populations with malT—, and another 12 with REL606 as a positive control.
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental design.

claim: The detection limit for OmpF+ genotypes in the original laboratory coevolution experiments was approximately 500 pfu/ml.
source: We based the threshold value on the detection limit of OmpF+ genotypes in the original laboratory coevolution experiments (~500 pfu/ml, see 'Coevolutionary Replay Experiments' section).
evidence: This is a direct statement about the experimental detection limit.

claim: Amplicon sequencing data have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject PRJNA646809.
source: Amplicon sequencing data used to generate fitness landscapes in this study have been deposited in the NCBI Sequence Read Archive under BioProject PRJNA646809.
evidence: This is a direct statement about data availability.
